items.prompt: What actually makes the sound when you speak?

options.label: Air rushing past the teeth produces the sound
options.feedback: Teeth help shape certain sounds afterward, but the buzzing sound itself starts further back, in the throat, before air ever reaches the teeth.

options.label: Two folds of tissue in the throat vibrate rapidly as air passes between them
options.feedback: That rapid fluttering chops the airflow into the pulses that the ear hears as a buzzing tone.

options.label: The lungs themselves vibrate to produce the sound
options.feedback: The lungs supply the moving air but do not vibrate to create sound; that vibration happens higher up, in the throat.

options.label: Sound comes from air bouncing off the roof of the mouth
options.feedback: The mouth's shape changes the sound afterwards, but nothing about air simply bouncing off the roof of the mouth creates the buzzing sound itself.

items.ok_line: That fluttering is exactly what turns moving air into sound.
items.ko_title: Not the teeth or the mouth
items.ko_line: The buzzing sound starts further back than the teeth or the roof of the mouth.
items.exp_title: A buzz made of two flaps of tissue
items.exp_text: Sitting across the airway in the throat are two folds of tissue, and when air from the lungs is pushed between them while they are drawn close together, they flutter rapidly open and shut. That fluttering chops the smooth, silent stream of air into a rapid series of little puffs, and it is those puffs, following one another very quickly, that the ear hears as a buzzing tone. Everything the mouth does afterwards shapes that buzz into recognisable speech, but the buzz itself starts at those two folds of tissue.

items.prompt: What changes inside your throat when you sing a higher note instead of a lower one?

options.label: More air is simply pushed out for a higher note
options.feedback: Pushing more air changes how loud a note is, not how high it is; pitch and loudness are controlled separately.

options.label: The mouth opens wider for a higher note
options.feedback: How wide the mouth opens shapes the sound's tone, but it isn't what determines whether a note is high or low.

options.label: Muscles pull the vocal cords tighter and shorter, making them vibrate faster
options.feedback: A tighter, shorter fold of tissue vibrates faster, and a faster vibration is heard as a higher note.

options.label: The vocal cords move further apart for a higher note
options.feedback: Moving the cords apart would let air pass without much vibration at all; producing any clear note needs them held close together.

items.ok_line: That change in tension and length is what raises the pitch.
items.ko_line: Pitch isn't set by how much air is pushed or how wide the mouth opens.
items.exp_text: The pitch of a vibrating fold of tissue depends on how fast it flutters back and forth, in the same way a tighter, shorter guitar string vibrates faster than a loose, long one. Small muscles in the throat can stretch the vocal cords tighter and effectively shorten the length that is free to vibrate, and both of those changes push the vibration rate up. A higher note is simply what a faster-vibrating fold of tissue sounds like.

items.prompt: What changes inside your throat when you speak more loudly instead of more softly?

options.label: The vocal cords simply vibrate faster for a louder sound
options.feedback: Vibrating faster changes pitch, not loudness; a note can be loud or soft at exactly the same pitch.

options.label: The mouth is opened much wider to speak loudly
options.feedback: Mouth opening shapes the sound's character, but a wide-open mouth by itself does not make a voice louder.

options.label: Louder speech comes from tensing the throat muscles further
options.feedback: Tensing those muscles changes pitch, not volume; loudness comes from how much air is pushed, not from how tight the cords are held.

options.label: More force is pushed from the lungs, making the vocal cords swing through a wider vibration
options.feedback: A wider swing with each flutter carries more sound energy outward, which is heard as greater loudness.

items.ok_line: Force from the lungs widens the swing, and a wider swing carries more sound.
items.ko_line: Loudness isn't set by vibration speed or how wide the mouth opens.
items.exp_title: A wider swing, not a faster one
items.exp_text: Loudness comes from how much energy is packed into each puff of air escaping between the vocal cords, and that energy comes from how forcefully the lungs push air up against them. Pushed harder, the cords are forced further apart with each flutter, swinging through a wider gap before snapping shut again, and a wider swing carries more sound energy outward. The rate of the vibration barely changes at all — what changes is how far each swing reaches.

items.prompt: Why do two people saying the exact same word never sound quite the same?

options.label: Their vocal cords are simply different colours
options.feedback: Vocal cords do not have any distinguishing colour that affects sound; what differs between people is size and shape, not colour.

options.label: The raw sound from the vocal cords is reshaped by resonating through the throat, mouth and nasal cavity, and the sizes of those spaces differ from person to person
options.feedback: Those differently sized resonating spaces boost different overtones in each person's voice, giving it its own character.

options.label: Only the loudness differs between two speakers
options.feedback: Two people can say a word at exactly the same loudness and still sound completely different, so loudness alone cannot be the explanation.

options.label: It depends only on how fast each person speaks
options.feedback: Even said at exactly the same speed, the same word still sounds different from one voice to the next, so speaking speed cannot be the reason either.

items.ok_title: A different room to resonate in
items.ok_line: Differently shaped resonating spaces give the same buzz a different character.
items.ko_line: None of those explains why the same word sounds different in two different voices.
items.exp_title: The same buzz, a different room
items.exp_text: The buzz made at the vocal cords is fairly plain on its own, and it only becomes a recognisable voice once it travels up through the throat, mouth and nasal passages. Each of those spaces acts like a small resonating chamber, boosting certain overtones in the buzz and damping others depending on its own particular size and shape. Because no two people's throats, mouths and sinuses are built to quite the same dimensions, the same starting buzz comes out sounding like a different voice each time.

items.prompt: What happens to your vocal cords when you whisper instead of speak normally?

options.label: The vocal cords vibrate, just more gently than usual
options.feedback: A whisper carries no vibrating tone at all; the cords are not vibrating gently, they are not vibrating.

options.label: The vocal cords are pulled tighter than usual
options.feedback: Tightening the cords would raise the pitch of a voiced sound; a whisper has no pitch at all because it has no vibration to begin with.

options.label: The vocal cords stay apart and never vibrate; air rushes through as a turbulent hiss instead
options.feedback: Air moving through that narrow, non-vibrating gap is exactly what produces a whisper's hiss instead of a buzzing tone.

options.label: Whispering uses the same vibration as speaking, only quieter
options.feedback: A quieter voiced sound is still a voiced sound with a pitch; a whisper is a completely different, toneless kind of sound.

items.ok_line: No vibration means no tone, just turbulence shaped into words.
items.ko_line: A whisper isn't a gentler version of ordinary voiced sound.
items.exp_title: A voice with no buzz in it
items.exp_text: Ordinary speech depends on the vocal cords being drawn close enough together that passing air sets them fluttering. For a whisper, the cords are held apart, close enough to narrow the airway but not close enough to vibrate, so air rushes through that narrow gap as a hiss of turbulence rather than a buzzing tone. The mouth still shapes that hiss into recognisable words, but without a vibrating source behind it, a whisper carries no pitch of its own.

items.prompt: How does your mouth turn a plain stream of air and sound into distinct consonants like 'p', 't', and 's'?

options.label: The tongue, lips and teeth briefly block or narrow the airflow at different points, shaping each interruption into a distinct sound
options.feedback: A brief block or narrowing at a particular point is exactly what gives each consonant its distinct character.

options.label: Each consonant comes from a different rate of vocal cord vibration
options.feedback: Vibration rate changes pitch, not which consonant is being said; consonants are shaped further forward, in the mouth.

options.label: Consonants come from changing how much air the lungs push out
options.feedback: How much air is pushed changes loudness, not which consonant sound comes out.

options.label: The nose alone is responsible for shaping every consonant
options.feedback: The nose plays a part in only a few sounds; most consonants are shaped entirely within the mouth, with the nasal passage closed off.

items.ok_line: Where and how the airflow is blocked is what makes each consonant distinct.
items.ko_title: Not pitch, volume or the nose alone
items.ko_line: Consonants come from where the mouth interrupts the airflow, not from these.
items.exp_text: A steady stream of air or a steady buzz from the vocal cords carries no consonants of its own; consonants are what happens when that stream gets interrupted in a particular way. Pressing the lips shut and releasing them gives a 'p', touching the tongue tip behind the teeth and releasing gives a 't', and narrowing a gap for air to hiss through gives an 's'. Every consonant is one of these characteristic interruptions, placed at a particular point along the mouth.

items.prompt: Why do 'm' and 'n' sound different from almost every other consonant, with a distinct humming quality?

options.label: The soft palate drops, opening a path into the nasal cavity so the sound resonates through the nose instead of being sealed inside the mouth
options.feedback: That open route into the nose is exactly what gives these sounds their humming quality.

options.label: 'm' and 'n' are made entirely inside the nose, without using the mouth at all
options.feedback: The mouth is still closed at a particular point to make these sounds; it's the escaping air's route afterward that makes them distinct.

options.label: They are produced by vibrating the nostrils directly
options.feedback: Nostrils do not vibrate to produce sound; the vibration still happens at the vocal cords, only the resonating path afterward changes.

options.label: They simply use a higher pitch than other consonants
options.feedback: 'm' and 'n' are not defined by being higher-pitched; their distinct quality comes from where the sound resonates, not from its pitch.

items.ok_line: Opening the route into the nasal cavity gives these sounds their hum.
items.ko_line: The humming quality comes from where the sound resonates, not from pitch or the nostrils themselves.
items.exp_text: For most sounds, a flap of soft tissue at the back of the throat, the soft palate, lifts to seal off the passage into the nose, keeping all the escaping air and sound routed out through the mouth. For 'm' and 'n', the mouth is closed at the lips or the tongue tip while that soft palate instead drops down, opening the route into the nasal cavity so the sound has nowhere to go but up and out through the nose. That detour through the nasal passage is what gives these sounds their distinct humming quality.

items.prompt: How does your mouth turn the same buzzing sound from your vocal cords into different vowels, like 'ee' and 'oo'?

options.label: Each vowel comes from a different rate of vocal cord vibration
options.feedback: Changing the vibration rate changes pitch, and a vowel like 'ee' can be said at any pitch at all; the vowel's identity comes from shaping afterward.

options.label: Moving the tongue and jaw reshapes the space the sound resonates through, favouring different overtones for each vowel
options.feedback: A differently shaped resonating space favours different overtones, and that is exactly what distinguishes one vowel from another.

options.label: The lungs release a specifically shaped puff of air for each vowel
options.feedback: The lungs simply supply a steady flow of air; it's what happens to that flow further up, in the throat and mouth, that gives each vowel its identity.

options.label: Vowels are distinguished only by how loudly they are said
options.feedback: 'ee' and 'oo' remain clearly different vowels whether whispered softly or said loudly, so loudness cannot be what separates them.

items.ok_line: Reshaping the mouth changes which overtones ring through.
items.ko_line: Vowels aren't set by pitch or by volume.
items.exp_title: The same buzz, a different shape around it
items.exp_text: The buzz from the vocal cords stays much the same no matter which vowel is being said; what changes is the shape of the space above it, formed by the tongue's position, how open the jaw is, and whether the lips are rounded. That changing shape favours different overtones within the buzz, damping some and letting others ring through more strongly, the way a differently shaped bottle changes the note you get blowing across its top. Each vowel is really the same source sound, filtered through a differently shaped mouth.

items.prompt: Why does your breathing pattern change while you are talking, compared with when you are simply sitting quietly?

options.label: Breathing becomes completely irregular and unpredictable while talking
options.feedback: Speech breathing follows a fairly consistent pattern, timed to the sentences being spoken, rather than being random.

options.label: You breathe in and out at exactly the same rate as when sitting quietly
options.feedback: The pattern noticeably changes for speech; it is not the same steady in-and-out rhythm as quiet resting breathing.

options.label: Breathing shifts to a quick in-breath followed by a long, controlled out-breath stretched across the words being spoken
options.feedback: Stretching the out-breath to match the length of what's being said is exactly what speech breathing requires.

options.label: Talking requires holding the breath completely until the sentence ends
options.feedback: Holding the breath would stop the airflow that the vocal cords need to keep vibrating; a sentence is spoken while air is still flowing out.

items.ok_line: A quick in-breath and a long, controlled out-breath match the shape of what's said.
items.ko_line: Speech breathing changes shape from resting breathing; it doesn't stay the same or stop altogether.
items.exp_text: Quiet resting breathing is fairly even, with the in-breath and the out-breath taking roughly the same amount of time. Speech needs a steady, unbroken stream of air pushed out across the vocal cords for as long as a phrase lasts, so the out-breath is stretched out and carefully controlled while the in-breath, snatched in the gaps between phrases, is comparatively quick. The whole rhythm of breathing reorganises itself around the shape of what is being said.

items.prompt: Why does a young child's voice sound so much higher-pitched than an adult's?

options.label: Children push far more air through the throat than adults do
options.feedback: Pushing more air would change loudness, not pitch, and children do not push unusually large amounts of air when they speak.

options.label: A child's throat resonates sound differently because it is a completely different shape
options.feedback: Resonance does shift a voice's character, but the sharp difference in pitch traces back to the vibrating cords themselves, not to the resonating spaces around them.

options.label: Children's vocal cords vibrate more slowly, which raises the pitch
options.feedback: A slower vibration produces a lower pitch, not a higher one; it is a faster vibration that gives a higher note.

options.label: A child's vocal cords are shorter, and shorter cords vibrate faster, producing a higher pitch
options.feedback: A shorter fold of tissue vibrating faster is exactly the same rule that gives any voice a higher note.

items.ok_line: Shorter vocal cords vibrate faster, and that's heard as a higher voice.
items.ko_title: Not more air or a slower vibration
items.ko_line: The higher pitch comes from cord length, not airflow or a slower flutter.
items.exp_title: The same rule, a smaller instrument
items.exp_text: Pitch depends on how fast the vocal cords flutter, and how fast they can flutter depends heavily on their length, in exactly the way a short string vibrates faster than a long one. A young child's vocal cords are considerably shorter than an adult's, so for the same amount of muscular tension they flutter at a noticeably faster rate. That faster flutter is heard as a higher-pitched voice, following the very same rule that lets a single adult voice slide from a low note to a high one.
